doc.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998

title: The three percent royalty contract
summary: Conniff received 'Begin the Beguine' as a single and signed a stock Columbia contract at three percent of the record price, netting about eighteen cents an album.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: anyway, so we did the Rosie sessions, and you asked — I still didn’t answer the question about the deal. So anyway when we got back — oh Mitch says I’m going to make it up to you when we get back, when we get back to New York. So that’s what he did. He gave me that single that I told you about, “Begin the Beguine” and “Stardust.” And that was the way he would wheel and deal, which developed into the album. So when the album came along, I said, “Well what’s the deal, Mitch.” And he said, “Oh don’t worry about the deal, you’ll talk to me all the time.” So they sent me contracts and I signed contracts, you know it’s the stock contract is what they say. So I signed a contract, it was three percent.

Three percent. Not three percent of an album, it’s three percent after you pay the cost of the jacket you know. These things here, these were selling for what, $3.98 or something back in those days. But the thing inside here.
No, but the thing inside was worth like maybe a dollar or so. That’s what you got the three percent on. But anyway.
Oh, wait a minute now, I want to make sure I understand this.
You didn’t get three percent of what they were actually selling it for. You got three percent of just the record.

The record itself — oh there were a lot of other little clauses. Like they used to be made of, what was it, acetate? They used to break. They had a ten percent breakage clause in there. You know the breakage clause is still in all the contracts? There is nothing that can break anymore. Now they say it’s because of the stuff that comes back or something. But anyway, yeah, you got three percent. Oh there were a lot of other things that cut it up. By the time I got all through, I think in those days I used to get eighteen cents on an album in those days. Now it’s up much more, and I have a better percentage. But anyway, to get back to your question about the deal, so after a while I was doing everything, you know “S’ Wonderful” “S’ Marvelous” “S’ Awful Nice” were out now. It’s a little later down the road. And they’re doing quite well, I’m getting gold records. And you know Justin Sogg and all them people were around, and one day I ran into Mitch and I said, “hey Mitch?” He says, “yeah?” We used to have a lot of arguments but we got along great. I says, “hey, what’s this contract these guys are giving me at Columbia?” He says, “what do you mean, what do you mean?” I said, “well I’m getting a three percent royalty. Doris Day and” — I can’t think of any names — give me some names in those days — well Sinatra, all of them, I said, “they’re getting five percent.” “Well that’s our top — you’re not getting the top royalty?
